In [[mathematics]], '''negative two''' or '''minus two''' is an [[integer]] two units from the [[origin (mathematics)|origin]],<ref>{{Cite book |author=Jeremko |first=Catherine V. |url=https://www.mobt3ath.com/uplode/book/book-21408.pdf |title=Just in time math |publisher=LearningExpress, LLC, New York |year=2003 |isbn=1-57685-506-6 |page=20 |access-date=August 21, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200326201758/https://www.mobt3ath.com/uplode/book/book-21408.pdf |archive-date=2020-03-26 |url-status=live}}</ref> denoted as −2<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Runesson |first1=Ulla |last2=Lövström |first2=Anna |last3=Hellquist |first3=Björn |date=2018-04-09 |title=Beyond the borders of the local: How "instructional products" from learning study can be shared and enhance student learning |url=http://www.emerald.com/ijlls/article/7/2/111-123/135438 |journal=International Journal for Lesson and Learning Studies |language=en |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=111–123 |doi=10.1108/IJLLS-01-2018-0004 |issn=2046-8253}}</ref> or <sup>−</sup>2.<ref>{{Cite book |author=Billstein |first1=Rick |title=A Problem Solving Approach to Mathematics for Elementary School Teachers |last2=Libeskind |first2=Shlomo |last3=Lott |first3=Johnny W. |publisher=Pearson Education, Inc |year=2010 |page=250}}</ref> It is the [[additive inverse]] of [[2]], following −3 and preceding [[−1]], and is the largest negative even integer. Except in rare cases exploring [[integral domain|integral ring]] [[prime element|prime elements]],<ref>{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A061019|name=Negate primes in factorization of n.}}</ref> negative two is generally not considered a [[prime number]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Can negative numbers be prime? |url=https://primes.utm.edu/notes/faq/negative_primes.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180123201057/http://primes.utm.edu/notes/faq/negative_primes.html |archive-date=January 23, 2018 |access-date=August 21, 2025 |publisher=primes.utm.edu}}</ref>

Negative two is sometimes used to denote the square reciprocal in the notation of [[International System of Units|SI]] base units, such as [[Metre per second squared|m·s<sup>−2</sup>]].<ref name="SIbrochure8th">{{SIbrochure8th}}</ref> Additionally, in fields like [[software design]], [[−1]] is often used as an invalid return value for functions,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Knuth |first=Donald |author-link=Donald Knuth |url=https://archive.org/details/artofcomputerpro02dona |title=The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1: Fundamental Algorithms |publisher=[[Addison-Wesley]] |year=1973 |isbn=0-201-03809-9 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/artofcomputerpro02dona/page/213 213]&ndash;214, also p. 631 |edition=second |access-date=August 21, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190403095951/https://archive.org/details/artofcomputerpro02dona/ |archive-date=April 3, 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref> and similarly, negative two may indicate other invalid conditions beyond negative one.<ref name="article yan2011joy">{{Cite journal |author=Yan |first1=Michael |last2=Leung |first2=Eric |last3=Han |first3=Binna |date=December 2011 |title=The Joy Of Engineering |url=http://web1.cs.columbia.edu/~sedwards/classes/2011/gateway-fall/reports/6-report.pdf |url-status=live |journal=Computer Science / Computer Engineering Final Report |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200321161819/http://web1.cs.columbia.edu/~sedwards/classes/2011/gateway-fall/reports/6-report.pdf |archive-date=March 21, 2020 |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref> For example, in the [[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]], negative one denotes non-existence, while negative two indicates an infinite solution.<ref>{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A164793|name=smallest number which has in its English name the letter "i" in the n-th position, −1 if such number no exist, −2 for infinite}}</ref><ref>{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A164805}}</ref>

== Properties ==
* Negative two is a complementary [[Bell number]] (also known as Rao Uppuluri-Carpenter numbers),<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |author-link=Eric W. Weisstein |title=Complementary Bell Number |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ComplementaryBellNumber.html |access-date=2025-08-21 |website=[[MathWorld]]--A Wolfram Web Resource |publisher=[[Wolfram Research]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Amdeberhan |first1=Tewodros |last2=De Angelis |first2=Valerio |last3=Moll |first3=Victor H. |chapter=Complementary Bell Numbers: Arithmetical Properties and Wilf's Conjecture |date=2013 |editor-last=Kotsireas |editor-first=Ilias S. |editor2-last=Zima |editor2-first=Eugene V. |title=Advances in Combinatorics |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-30979-3_2 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=23–56 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-30979-3_2 |isbn=978-3-642-30979-3}}</ref> and a [[Hermite number]].
* Negative two makes the [[Ideal class group|class number]] of the [[quadratic field]] <math>\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt{d}]</math> equal to 1, meaning its [[ring of integers]] is a [[unique factorization domain]].<ref group="Note">When <math>d<0</math>, if the ring of integers of <math>\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt{d}]</math> is a unique factorization domain, all numbers in <math>\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt{d}]</math> have a unique factorization. For example, <math>\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt{-5}]</math> is not, as 6 can be factored in two ways in <math>\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]</math>: <math>2\times 3</math> and <math>(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})</math>.</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hardy |first1=Godfrey Harold |author1-link=G. H. Hardy |url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontoth00hard |title=An introduction to the theory of numbers |last2=Wright |first2=E. M. |publisher=The Clarendon Press Oxford University Press |year=1979 |isbn=978-0-19-853171-5 |edition=Fifth |page=213 |mr=568909 |access-date=August 21, 2025 |orig-year=1938}}</ref> According to the [[Stark–Heegner theorem]], only nine negative numbers have this property,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Conway |first=John Horton |author-link=John Horton Conway |url=https://archive.org/details/bookofnumbers0000conw/page/224 |title=The Book of Numbers |author2=Guy, Richard K. |publisher=Springer |year=1996 |isbn=0-387-97993-X |page=[https://archive.org/details/bookofnumbers0000conw/page/224 224] |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |author=H.M. Stark |date=January 1969 |title=On the "gap" in a theorem of Heegner |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0022314X69900237 |url-status=live |journal=Journal of Number Theory |language=en |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=16–27 |doi=10.1016/0022-314X(69)90023-7 |bibcode=1969JNT.....1...16S |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200628181801/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0022314X69900237 |archive-date=June 28, 2020 |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |author-link=Eric W. Weisstein |title=Heegner Number |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/HeegnerNumber.html |access-date=2025-08-21 |website=MathWorld--A Wolfram Web Resource |publisher=[[Wolfram Research]], Inc. |language=en}}</ref> corresponding to [[Heegner number|Heegner numbers]].<ref>{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A003173|name=Heegner numbers: imaginary quadratic fields with unique factorization (or class number 1).}}</ref>
** Negative two also makes the quadratic field <math>\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt{d}]</math> a simple Euclidean field (or norm-Euclidean field).<ref name="misc bradford2014unit">{{Cite journal |author=Kyle Bradford |last2=Eugen J. Ionascu |year=2014 |title=Unit Fractions in Norm-Euclidean Rings of Integers |journal=Acta Mathematica Universitatis Comenianae |arxiv=1405.4025 }}</ref> Only five negative numbers have this property: −11, −7, −3, −2, −1.<ref>{{Cite book |last=LeVeque |first=William J. |author-link=William J. LeVeque |url=https://archive.org/details/topicsinnumberth0000leve/page/ |title=Topics in Number Theory, Volumes I and II |publisher=Dover Publications |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-486-42539-9 |location=New York |pages=[https://archive.org/details/topicsinnumberth0000leve/page/ II:57,81] |zbl=1009.11001 |access-date=August 21, 2025 |orig-year=1956}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=A048981 - OEIS |url=https://oeis.org/A048981 |access-date=2025-08-21 |website=oeis.org}}</ref> If relaxed, −15 is included.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Kelly Emmrich and Clark Lyons |date=December 18, 2017 |title=Norm-Euclidean Ideals in Galois Cubic Fields |url=https://wcnt.files.wordpress.com/2017/12/wcnt2017-kellyclark.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200326161042/https://wcnt.files.wordpress.com/2017/12/wcnt2017-kellyclark.pdf |archive-date=March 26, 2020 |access-date=August 21, 2025 |publisher=2017 West Coast Number Theory Conference}}</ref><ref>{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A296818|name=Squarefree values of n for which the quadratic field Q[ sqrt(n) ] possesses a norm-Euclidean ideal class.}}</ref>
* Negative two is the largest negative number unreachable from 1 in two steps using addition, subtraction, or multiplication.<ref name="A229686">{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A229686|name=The negative number of minimum absolute value not obtainable from 1 in n steps using addition, multiplication, and subtraction.}}</ref> The largest in one step is −1, and in three steps, −4.<ref name="A229686"/> This relates to the [[straight-line program]] combined with addition, subtraction, and multiplication,<ref name="article koiran2005valiant">{{Cite journal |author=Koiran, Pascal |year=2005 |title=Valiant's model and the cost of computing integers |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00037-004-0186-2 |journal=Computational Complexity |publisher=Springer |volume=13 |issue=3–4 |pages=131–146 |doi=10.1007/s00037-004-0186-2 |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref> exploring the algebraic complexity of integers in relation to NP = P.<ref name="shub1994intractability">{{Cite journal |author=Shub |first1=Michael |last2=Smale |first2=Steve |year=1995 |title=On the intractability of Hilbert's Nullstellensatz and an algebraic version of "NP= P?" |url=https://shub.ccny.cuny.edu/articles/1995-Intractability_of_Hilberts_Nullstellensatz.pdf |journal=Duke Mathematical Journal |volume=81 |issue=1 |page=47-54 |doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-95-08105-8 |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref>
* Negative two is the second-order i.e., <math>H_2 = H_2(0) = -2</math>.<ref>{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A067994|name=Hermite numbers}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Hermite numbers |url=https://planetmath.org/hermitenumbers |date=March 22, 2013 |author=pahio |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150919001120/http://planetmath.org/hermitenumbers |archive-date=September 19, 2015 |access-date=August 21, 2025 |publisher=planetmath.org |url-status=live |trans-title=Hermite numbers}}</ref>
* Negative two makes <math>k(k+1)(k+2)</math> a [[triangular number]].<ref name="Figurate Numbers§D3">{{Cite book |author=Richard K. Guy |title="Figurate Numbers", §D3 in Unsolved Problems in Number Theory |publisher=Springer-Verlag |year=1994 |isbn=978-0387208602 |edition=2nd |series=Problem Books in Mathematics |location=New York |page=148}}</ref> Only nine integers have this property, with negative two being the smallest: −2, −1, 0, 1, 4, 5, 9, [[56 (number)|56]], and [[636 (number)|636]].<ref name="A165519">{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A165519|name=Integers k for which k(k+1)(k+2) is a triangular number.}}</ref>

=== Divisors of negative two ===
The divisors of negative two, including negative [[divisors]], are identical to those of two: −2, −1, 1, 2. By definition, negative numbers are not typically subjected to [[Prime number#Unique factorization|prime factorization]], though <math>-1</math> can be factored out as <math>-1 \times 2</math>,<ref name="book bard2015sage">{{Cite book |author=Bard, G.V. |url=https://www.faculty.luther.edu/~bernatzr/Courses/M351/sage_for_ug_color.pdf |title=Sage for Undergraduates |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=2015 |isbn=9781470411114 |page=269 |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref> making 2 a [[Prime number|prime factor]] but not the result of prime factorization. As a [[Gaussian integer]], negative two can be factored as <math>i \times (1+i)^2</math>, where <math>1+i</math> is a [[Table of Gaussian integer factorizations|Gaussian prime]] and <math>i</math> is the [[imaginary unit]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dresden |first1=Greg |last2=Dymàček |first2=Wayne M. |date=2005 |title=Finding Factors of Factor Rings over the Gaussian Integers |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/30037545 |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=112 |issue=7 |pages=602–611 |doi=10.2307/30037545 |jstor=30037545 |issn=0002-9890}}</ref>

=== Powers of negative two ===
The first few powers of negative two are −2, 4, −8, 16, −32, 64, −128, oscillating between positive and negative.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Wells |first=Chauncey H. |date=1963 |title=Using a negative base for number notation |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/27956751 |journal=The Mathematics Teacher |publisher=National Council of Teachers of Mathematics |volume=56 |issue=2 |pages=91–93 |doi=10.5951/MT.56.2.0091 |jstor=27956751 |issn=0025-5769}}</ref> The positive terms are powers of four, and the negative terms differ from powers of four by a factor of negative two.<ref>{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A004171}}</ref> This property makes negative two the largest negative number that can represent all real numbers as a base without using a negative sign or [[two's complement]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Knuth |first=Donald |title=[[The Art of Computer Programming]], Volume 2 |year=1998 |edition=3rd |pages=204–205}} Knuth mentions both negabinary and negadecimal.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |author=Petkovsek |first=Marko |date=May 1990 |title=Ambiguous Numbers are Dense |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2324393 |url-status=live |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=97 |issue=5 |pages=408–411 |doi=10.2307/2324393 |jstor=2324393 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200610052816/https://www.jstor.org/stable/2324393?origin=crossref |archive-date=June 10, 2020 |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A122803|name=Powers of −2}}</ref> In 1957, some computers used a base-negative-two numeral system for calculations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Marczynski |first1=R.W. |title=The First Seven Years of Polish Digital Computers |journal=IEEE Annals of the History of Computing |date=1980 |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=37–48 |url=http://chc60.fgcu.edu/images/articles/Marczynski.pdf |doi=10.1109/MAHC.1980.10008 |bibcode=1980IAHC....2a..37M |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719192337/http://chc60.fgcu.edu/images/articles/Marczynski.pdf |archive-date=19 July 2011 }}</ref> Similarly, using <math>2i</math> can represent complex numbers.<ref>{{Cite journal |author=Braunwart |first=Robert |date=April 1965 |title=Negative and Imaginary Radices |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1949-8594.1965.tb13422.x |url-status=live |journal=School Science and Mathematics |language=en |volume=65 |issue=4 |pages=292–295 |doi=10.1111/j.1949-8594.1965.tb13422.x |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220627051548/https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1949-8594.1965.tb13422.x |archive-date=June 27, 2022 |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref>

The [[Geometric Series of −2|sum of the powers of negative two]] is a [[divergent geometric series]]. Although divergent, its generalized sum is <math>\frac{1}{3}</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Leibniz |first=Gottfried |author-link=Gottfried Leibniz |url=http://www.nlb-hannover.de/Leibniz/Leibnizarchiv/Veroeffentlichungen/ |title=Sämtliche Schriften und Briefe, Reihe 7, Band 3: 1672–1676: Differenzen, Folgen, Reihen |publisher=Akademie Verlag |year=2003 |isbn=3-05-004003-3 |editor-last=Probst |editor-first=S. |pages=205–207 |access-date=August 21, 2025 |editor2-last=Knobloch |editor2-first=E. |editor3-last=Gädeke |editor3-first=N. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131017093457/http://www.nlb-hannover.de/Leibniz/Leibnizarchiv/Veroeffentlichungen/ |archive-date=October 17, 2013 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Knobloch |first=Eberhard |author-link=Eberhard Knobloch |date=2006-02-01 |title=Beyond Cartesian limits: Leibniz's passage from algebraic to "transcendental" mathematics |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0315086004000199 |journal=Historia Mathematica |series=The Origins of Algebra: From al-Khwarizmi to Descartes |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=113–131 |doi=10.1016/j.hm.2004.02.001 |issn=0315-0860 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191014164204/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0315086004000199 |archive-date=October 14, 2019}}</ref>
:<math>\sum_{k=0}^{n} (-2)^k = 1 - 2 + 4 - 8 + \dots</math>
Using the [[geometric series]] formula,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |author-link=Eric W. Weisstein |title=Geometric Series |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/GeometricSeries.html |access-date=2025-08-21 |website=MathWorld--A Wolfram Web Resource |publisher=[[Wolfram Research]], Inc. |language=en}}</ref>
:<math>\sum_{k=0}^\infty a r^k = \frac{a}{1-r}</math>
with the first term <math>a=1</math> and common ratio <math>r=-2</math>, the result is <math>\frac{1}{3}</math>. However, the series is divergent, with partial sums:<ref name="oeisa07">{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A077925}}</ref>
:1, −1, 3, −5, 11, −21, 43, −85, 171, −341...<ref name="oeisa07" />
Though divergent, [[Euler]] assigned the value <math>\frac{1}{3}</math> to this series,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Euler |first=Leonhard |author-link=Leonhard Euler |url=http://www.math.dartmouth.edu/~euler/pages/E212.html |title=Institutiones calculi differentialis cum eius usu in analysi finitorum ac doctrina serierum |year=1755 |page=234 |access-date=August 21, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080225150938/http://www.math.dartmouth.edu/~euler/pages/E212.html |archive-date=February 25, 2008 |url-status=live}}</ref> known as [[Euler summation]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Korevaar |first=Jacob |url=https://archive.org/details/tauberiantheoryc00kore |title=Tauberian Theory: A Century of Developments |publisher=Springer |year=2004 |isbn=3-540-21058-X |page=[https://archive.org/details/tauberiantheoryc00kore/page/n337 325] |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref>

=== Negative second power ===
The negative second power of a number is its square reciprocal, applicable to functions as well.<ref name="phdthesis 孙长军2004负二次幂函数与排列数的交错级数型线性微分方程">{{Cite journal |author=Sun Changjun |year=2004 |title=Fù èrcì mì hánshù yǔ páiliè shù de jiāocuò jíshù xíng xiànxìng wēifēn fāngchéng |script-title=zh:负二次幂函数与排列数的交错级数型线性微分方程 |trans-title=Negative Second Power Functions and Alternating Series Type Linear Differential Equations of Permutation Numbers |url=https://kns.cnki.net/kcms/detail/detail.aspx?dbcode=CJFQ&filename=SDGC200405019 |journal=Shandong Ligong Daxue Xuebao (Ziran Kexue Ban) (自然科学版) (连云港职业技术学院数学教研室) |language=zh |publisher=Lianyungang Vocational Technical College Mathematics Department |issue=5 |pages=85–89 |id=SDGC200405019 |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref> In daily life, it is occasionally used to denote units without a division sign, such as acceleration, typically written as m/s<sup>2</sup> but also as m·s<sup>−2</sup> in [[International System of Units|SI]] notation.<ref name="SIbrochure8th"/>

Common topics related to the square reciprocal include: for any real number <math>n</math>, its square reciprocal <math>n^{-2}</math> is always positive; the [[inverse-square law]];<ref name="Hooke1680">{{Cite journal |author=Koyré |first=Alexandre |date=December 1952 |title=An Unpublished Letter of Robert Hooke to Isaac Newton |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/348155 |journal=Isis |language=en |volume=43 |issue=4 |pages=312–337 |doi=10.1086/348155 |pmid=13010921 |issn=0021-1753 |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref> grid turbulence decay;<ref name="2013中国近代航空工业史">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rYx9DwAAQBAJ&pg=PT378 |title=Zhōngguó jìndài hángkōng gōngyè shǐ (1909–1949) |publisher=Aviation Industry Press |year=2013 |isbn=9787516502617 |series=China Aviation Industry History Series: General History |script-title=zh:中国近代航空工业史（1909-1949） |trans-title=History of Modern Chinese Aviation Industry (1909-1949) |lccn=2019437836 |access-date=August 21, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201130100258/https://books.google.com.tw/books?id=rYx9DwAAQBAJ&pg=PT378#v=onepage&q&f=false |archive-date=November 30, 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref> and the [[Basel problem]].<ref name="HAVIL-GAMMA">{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/gammaexploringeu00havi |title=Gamma: Exploring Euler's Constant |last=Havil |first=J. |date=2003 |publisher=Princeton University Press |location=Princeton, New Jersey |isbn=0-691-09983-9 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/gammaexploringeu00havi/page/n60 37]–42 (Chapter 4) |trans-title=Gamma: Exploring Euler's Constant |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref> The Basel problem states that the sum of the square reciprocals of natural numbers converges to <math>\frac{\pi^2}{6}</math>:<ref>{{Cite web |title=Evaluating {{math|''ζ''(2)}} |url=http://secamlocal.ex.ac.uk/people/staff/rjchapma/etc/zeta2.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070629174127/http://www.secamlocal.ex.ac.uk/people/staff/rjchapma/etc/zeta2.pdf |archive-date=June 29, 2007 |access-date=August 21, 2025 |publisher=secamlocal.ex.ac.uk |url-status=live |trans-title=Evaluating ζ(2)}}</ref><ref name="HAVIL-GAMMA"/>
:<math>\sum^{\infin}_{n=1} {n^{-2}} = {1^{-2} }+{2^{-2} }+{3^{-2} }+\cdots = {1 \over 1^2 }+{1 \over 2^2 }+{1 \over 3^2 }+\cdots = { \pi^2 \over 6 }</math>
This value equals the [[Riemann zeta function]] at 2.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Xu Zhinong |title=Xiūxián shùxué de lànshǎng ... Zhōngguó de Luòshū |script-title=zh:休閒數學的濫觴⋯中國的洛書 |trans-title=The Origin of Recreational Mathematics: China's Luoshu |url=https://www.lungteng.com.tw/Web/Upload/Upload_File/Source13/math020.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200321071742/https://www.lungteng.com.tw/Web/Upload/Upload_File/Source13/math020.pdf |archive-date=March 21, 2020 |access-date=August 21, 2025 |publisher=lungteng.com.tw}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author= |title=Bāsài'ěr wèntí (Basel problem) de duōzhǒng jiěfǎ |script-title=zh:巴塞尔问题(Basel problem)的多种解法 |trans-title=Multiple Solutions to the Basel Problem |url=http://www.cnblogs.com/misaka01034/p/BaselProof.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190502071905/http://www.cnblogs.com/misaka01034/p/BaselProof.html |archive-date=May 2, 2019 |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref>

For any real number, the square reciprocal is positive. For negative two, it is <math>\frac{1}{4}</math>. The square reciprocals of the first few [[Natural number|natural numbers]] are:

=== Square root of negative two ===
The square root of negative two, defined with the [[imaginary unit]] <math>i</math> satisfying <math>i^2 = -1</math>, is derived from <math>\sqrt{-x} = \pm i \sqrt{x}</math>. For negative two, it is <math>\sqrt{-2} = \pm i \sqrt{2}</math>.<ref group="Note" name="Z_R Knuth bi-imaginary">In the bi-imaginary number system <math>\left\langle\sqrt{R},Z_R\right\rangle</math>, where <math>R</math> is negative two and <math>Z_R</math> is two, it is <math>\left\langle\pm \mathrm i \sqrt{2},Z_2\right\rangle</math>. {{Cite journal |author=Donald E. Knuth |date=April 1, 1960 |title=A imaginary number system |trans-title=A imaginary number system |url=http://portal.acm.org/citation.cfm?doid=367177.367233 |journal=Communications of the ACM |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=245–247 |doi=10.1145/367177.367233 |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Knuth |first=Donald E. |date=1960-04-01 |title=A imaginary number system |url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/367177.367233 |journal=Commun. ACM |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=245–247 |doi=10.1145/367177.367233 |issn=0001-0782 |quote=Bi-imaginary number system}}</ref><ref name="Knuth2">{{Cite book |last=Knuth |first=Donald |author-link=Donald Knuth |title=The art of computer programming |publisher=Addison-Wesley |year=1998 |isbn=0-201-89684-2 |edition=3rd |volume=2 |location=Boston |pages=205 |chapter=Positional Number Systems |oclc=48246681}}</ref><ref name="inproceedings slekys1978modified">{{Cite book |author=Slekys |first1=Arunas G |title=1978 IEEE 4th Symposium onomputer Arithmetic (ARITH) |last2=Avižienis |first2=Algirdas |publisher=IEEE |year=1978 |page=48-55 |chapter=A modified bi-imaginary number system |doi=10.1109/ARITH.1978.6155756}}</ref><ref name="article slekys1976design">{{Cite journal |author=Slekys, Arunas George |year=1976 |title=Design of complex number digital arithmetic units based on a modified bi-imaginary number system. |journal=University of California, Los Angeles}}</ref> The principal value is <math>\sqrt{-2} = i \sqrt{2}</math>.<ref group="Note">The principal value of the square root of –2 is  <math>\sqrt{-x} = \pm i \sqrt{x}</math> taking the positive value; with respect to –2, that is <math>\sqrt{-2} = i \sqrt{2}</math>.</ref><ref name=":1" /><ref name="Knuth2"/><ref name="inproceedings slekys1978modified"/><ref name="article slekys1976design"/>

== Representation ==
Negative two is typically represented by adding a negative sign before 2,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kreith |first1=Kurt |last2=Mendle |first2=Al |date=2013-04-18 |title=Toward A Coherent Treatment of Negative Numbers |url=https://journals.library.columbia.edu/index.php/jmetc/article/view/775 |journal=Journal of Mathematics Education at Teachers College |language=en |volume=4 |issue=1 |page=53 |doi=10.7916/jmetc.v4i1.775 |issn=2156-1397}}</ref> commonly called "negative two" or "minus two" in English.<ref>{{Cite journal |author=Walter Noll |date=March 2003 |title=Mathematics should not be boring |trans-title=Mathematics should not be boring |url=http://www.math.cmu.edu/~wn0g/mnb.pdf |url-status=live |journal=CMU Math - Carnegie Mellon University |page=13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160322134616/http://www.math.cmu.edu/~wn0g/mnb.pdf |archive-date=March 22, 2016 |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref>

In [[Binary number|binary]], especially in computing, negative numbers are often represented using [[two's complement]].<ref>{{Cite book |quote=Signed integers are two's complement binary values that can be used to represent both positive and negative integer values. |date=October 2025 |section=4.2.1 Integers |title=Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual - Volume 1: Basic Architecture |page=4-3 <!-- 4 'dash' 3 --> |url=https://cdrdv2.intel.com/v1/dl/getContent/671436 }}</ref> Negative two is represented as "...11111110<sub>(2)</sub>", specifically "1110<sub>(2)</sub>" for 4-bit, "11111110<sub>(2)</sub>" for 8-bit, and "1111111111111110<sub>(2)</sub>" for 16-bit integers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=3.9. Two's Complement |url=http://www.cs.uwm.edu/classes/cs151/Bacon/Lecture/HTML/ch03.html |website=Chapter 3. Data Representation |date=December 3, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201130205628/http://www.cs.uwm.edu/classes/cs151/Bacon/Lecture/HTML/ch03.html |archive-date=November 30, 2020 |access-date=August 21, 2025 |publisher=cs.uwm.edu |url-status=live |trans-title=3.9. Two's Complement}}</ref> In signed notation, it is "−10<sub>(2)</sub>".<ref>David J. Lilja and Sachin S. Sapatnekar, ''Designing Digital Computer Systems with Verilog'', Cambridge University Press, 2005 [https://books.google.com/books?vid=ISBN052182866X&id=5BvW0hYhxkQC&pg=PA37&lpg=PA37&ots=l-E0VjyPt8&dq=%22two%27s+complement+arithmetic%22&sig=sS5_swrfrzcQI2nHWest75sIjgg online] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190726000000/https://books.google.com/books?vid=ISBN052182866X&id=5BvW0hYhxkQC&pg=PA37&lpg=PA37&ots=l-E0VjyPt8&dq=%22two%27s+complement+arithmetic%22&sig=sS5_swrfrzcQI2nHWest75sIjgg}}</ref>

== Plus or minus two ==
Plus or minus two (<math>\pm 2</math>) is expressed using the [[Plus–minus sign|plus-minus sign]], representing both positive and negative two. It denotes the [[square roots]] of 4 or the solutions to the [[quadratic equation]] <math>x^2 = 4</math>, i.e., <math>\sqrt{4} = \pm{2}</math>. Plus or minus two appears more frequently in cultural contexts, such as [[music composition|music compositions]]<ref name="article pace1998positive">{{Cite journal |author=Pace, Ian |year=1998 |title=Positive or negative 2 |trans-title=Positive or negative 2 |journal=The Musical Times |publisher=JSTOR |volume=139 |issue=1860 |pages=4–15 |doi=10.2307/1004287 |jstor=1004287 }}</ref> or the documentary ±2 °C, which explores the environmental impact of a [[climate change|global temperature change]] of two degrees.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Tang |first1=Jialing |last2=Liu |first2=Liren |last3=Chen |first3=Peiling |date=March 4, 2010 |title=Zhèng-fù èr dù C shùjù jiědú cuòwù, xuézhě bù bèishū |script-title=zh:正負2度Ｃ數據解讀錯誤 學者不背書 |trans-title=Data Misinterpretation in ±2&nbsp;°C, Scholars Do Not Endorse |url=http://www.libertytimes.com.tw/2010/new/mar/4/today-life19.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100307041132/http://www.libertytimes.com.tw/2010/new/mar/4/today-life19.htm |archive-date=March 7, 2010 |access-date=August 21, 2025 |publisher=[[Liberty Times]] |language=zh-tw}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author=Zhu Liqun |date=March 3, 2010 |title=Huán tuán kēxué jǔzhèng ± èr dù C nèiróng yǒu wù |script-title=zh:環團科學舉證 ±2&nbsp;°C內容有誤 |trans-title=Environmental Groups and Scientists Point Out Errors in ±2&nbsp;°C |url=http://www.tcsh.mlc.edu.tw:8080/dept/Share/L-3.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141026151652/http://www.tcsh.mlc.edu.tw:8080/dept/Share/L-3.html |archive-date=October 26, 2014 |access-date=August 21, 2025 |publisher=[[China Times]] |language=zh-tw}}</ref>
